bib.title: Chapter 8. Improving How an Agent Learns (Reinforcement Learning: Industrial Applications of Intelligent Agents)

question: How can an RL practitioner improve learning by revisiting the MDP assumptions, adding hierarchy, multiple agents, expert guidance, and other paradigms?
contributions: Survey of MDP variants (POMDP, contextual MDP, changing action sets, regularized MDP)
Overview of hierarchical RL (HIRO, DIAYN, HAAR)
Overview of MARL (Markov games vs extensive-form games, centralized vs decentralized, MADDPG, TD hysteresis, Dec-HDRQN)
Overview of expert guidance (behavior cloning, DQfD, GAIL, SQIL, inverse RL, curriculum learning, residual RL)
Brief notes on meta-learning and transfer learning

results.claim: A POMDP can be turned back into an MDP by adding a state estimator that predicts a belief state; the simplest common approach is an RNN at the end of the state representation function.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own
results.quote: slap on a recurrent neural network (RNN) at the end of the state representation function
results.where: Rethinking the MDP / Predicting the belief state

results.claim: Atari benchmarks stack four frames of pixel observations to keep some history of the environment.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own; example of putting past observations in the state
results.quote: Atari benchmarks always stack four frames of pixel observations in order

results.claim: In a simulated four-way intersection an LSTM-enabled POMDP policy learns when to set off, avoiding collisions through an engineered reward.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own; Qiao et al. 2018, simulation only
results.where: Case Study: Using POMDPs in Autonomous Vehicles

results.claim: Regularizers such as SAC's alter the Bellman equality, but Li et al. proved convergence holds for any regularizer that follows some rules.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own

results.claim: HIRO splits the policy: the low-level policy gets an intrinsic (distance-to-state) reward from the high-level policy, which gets the environment reward and samples at a slower rate; Nachum et al. relabel high-level goals in the replay buffer to fix off-policy staleness.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own; legged simulated robot
results.quote: The high-level policy samples at a slower rate than the low-level policy to provide a temporal abstraction.

results.claim: DIAYN promotes unsupervised discovery of distinguishable, diverse low-level skills (e.g. HalfCheetah running, crawling, sitting).
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own

results.claim: HAAR uses the high-level advantage estimate, not Euclidean distance to state, as the reward to retrain pretrained low-level skills.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own
results.quote: advantage estimate from the high-level policy

results.claim: HRL helps when the agent is complex; where the environment is the complex part, HRL may not be beneficial.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own

results.claim: Decentralized MARL with single-agent algorithms is nonstationary from each agent's view; basic experience replay does not help and policies are usually suboptimal and may not converge as complexity grows.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own
results.quote: nonstationary from the perspective of any single agent

results.claim: Cui, Liu and Nallanathan used independent Q-learning in a simulation of three UAVs with fixed positions, with no correction for nonstationarity.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own; UAV wireless-network simulation
results.quote: and solve in a simulation of three UAVs.
results.where: Case Study: Using Single-Agent Decentralized Learning in UAVs

results.claim: MADDPG uses a centralized critic over all agents' actions with local actors, handling cooperative and competitive settings; it learns other agents' policies and damps nonstationarity by updating a limited random subset of policies.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own
results.quote: updating a limited subset of random policies

results.claim: Temporal-difference hysteresis applies a smaller learning rate when the TD error is below a threshold (usually zero), biasing agents to optimism.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own
results.quote: a slower (smaller) update rate is applied

results.claim: Dec-HDRQN combines DQN, hysteresis and a replay buffer synchronized over all agents (trajectories for RNN training).
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own

results.claim: MARL has no convergence guarantees for nontrivial environments because optimality is hard to define.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own

results.claim: There were more than 50 new MARL papers on arXiv in June 2020.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own; author's count, method not given
results.quote: there were more than 50 new MARL research

results.claim: Behavior cloning is not popular because it overfits the expert demonstrations and fails in undemonstrated states.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own

results.claim: SQIL simplifies DQfD and GAIL by controlling replay-buffer trajectories, reconstructing rewards for them and using a loss that stays near expert trajectories; Winder suggests the amount of expert advice could be controlled by weighting the regularization (his idea, not stated as SQIL's result).
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own
results.quote: You could even control the amount of expert advice to use

results.claim: IRL replaces manual reward design by learning a reward from demonstrations, but repeatedly retrains RL so it does not scale beyond simple state spaces; failed demonstrations can be included by demoting their reward.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own

results.claim: There are three types of transfer: same task and domain, same domain different task, and across domains.
results.setup: Winder ch. 8, industrial-RL overview; no experiments of the author's own
results.quote: Fundamentally there are three types of transfer.

limits: Overview chapter: the author states that a full treatment of each theme would take another book.
No experiments, hyperparameters or benchmark numbers of its own; results are described qualitatively from cited papers.
Written in 2020: 'recent' MARL, HRL, meta-RL and IRL work is pre-LLM; says nothing on RLHF or LLM agents.
Author's views are flagged as opinion (e.g. 'I suspect', 'I can imagine').
practices: Check whether the MDP assumptions hold; if the state is partly hidden, model a POMDP and add history or an RNN (Rethinking the MDP).
Model context that is fixed per episode as a contextual MDP (Contextual MDPs).
Design the hierarchy manually when concerns separate clearly before reaching for learned hierarchies (Naive HRL).
Consider an initial library of skills or pretraining; it could improve learning speed (HRL Conclusions, TIP).

Choose centralized learning with decentralized execution for sample efficiency, decentralized learning when communication is unreliable or agents differ (Centralized or Decentralized; difficulties box).
Take time defining the problem: a small change to a MARL problem can force starting again (MARL Conclusions, TIP).
Include failed demonstrations in IRL by demoting their reward (Inverse RL).
Reduce high-dimensional state with autoencoding or hashing before IRL (Inverse RL).
Reuse earlier policies and experience rather than training from scratch (Transfer Learning).

the set of actions available at a certain time, modeled as a random variable
